unit.why: A short anecdote: a householder asks the holy rabbi to come to his house tomorrow, and the rabbi refuses to promise, explaining that prayer involves self-sacrifice; a moral lesson follows.
unit.boundary_note: the division ends with the section heading 'מענין הגאולה', which belongs to the next division

stories.start_quote: פ״א ביקש בעה״ב אחד את מהה״צ
stories.summary_en: When a householder asks the tsaddik R. Sh. K. to come to his house tomorrow, the tsaddik calls him a fool and refuses to promise: the evening Shema, sleep, the morning prayer and falling on the face each involve self-sacrifice, and God may grant his wish to give up his life; the text then concludes that a person must cast off evil desires and seek only to sanctify God's name.

quotes: הלא צריך היום להתפלל ערבית ולקרות ק״ש
ויש בהתפלה כמה עולמות עד שבאים לק״ש
tags.why: the tsaddik's refusal rests on what the coming prayers demand of him
a minimal anecdote wrapped in a homiletic conclusion ('כללו של דבר')

quotes: שצריך האדם לבטל ממנו כל התאוות רעות
tags.why: the concluding lesson calls for nullifying evil desires

quotes: רק לראות שיקודש על ידו שם שמים
tags.why: the moral point is sanctifying God's name and casting off bad traits

quotes: ושמא יתן הקב״ה שימלא לי רצוני
tags.why: the tsaddik hopes to expire in prayer, a sign of total attachment to God
the tsaddik deals with an ordinary householder; his affiliation is unclear

missing_concepts: mesirut nefesh (self-sacrifice) in the Shema and in falling on the face
refusing to promise future actions (not committing about tomorrow)
